newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan hostage ambassador hits back at critics.
newsitem.headline: Japan hostage ambassador hits back at critics.

text.p: Japan's former ambassador to Peru, sacked last week following the Lima hostage crisis, has hit back at his critics, saying he has been treated like a war criminal since his return home.

Initially hailed as a hero who stoutly defended fellow hostages during the 127-day siege at his residence in Lima, Morihisa Aoki fell from grace on his return home when the spotlight switched from the fate of the captives to how the incident happened.
Aoki, who was fired from his post last week to take responsibility for the crisis but remains in Japan's Foreign Ministry, lashed back in an article published in Wednesday's Asahi Shimbun.
"I was heralded as a 'samurai diplomat' during captivity and treated like an A-class war criminal upon my return to Japan," wrote Aoki. "I am not a hero, but nor am I a coward."
Aoki defended himself against Japanese media criticism that in his first news conference in Lima after his release his demeanour did not show the solemnity that was required.
Media reports criticised his combative manner of responding to questions and accused him of lacking dignity by chain-smoking throughout the briefing.
"I wanted to convey to the world at the news conference that the Japanese are not weaklings who panic after long captivity," Aoki said.
Responding to criticism that he failed to negotiate with the rebels to free the hostages from captivity, Aoki said a hostage was in no position to negotiate.
"As the incident dragged on, the one and most important duty of a hostage was to stay alive and healthy.
"I shifted down my mental gear and tried not to think of difficult things...only which noodles to eat in the morning or what moves to make in chess," he said.
Aoki also defended his decision to hold the December 17 reception that was taken over by Marxist rebels who initially took about 500 guests hostage.
"I cannot escape the responsibility for inviting the incident, but security (in Peru) had definitely improved and inviting as many people as possible was an obvious choice," Aoki said.
"My sincere wish now is that people will not desert Peru because of this incident."
Most of the hostages, except for Aoki and 71 others, were released in the weeks before the siege was finally ended by an April 22 raid by Peruvian commandos.
Two commandos and a hostage -- as well as all 14 rebels -- died in the assault.
